packet.headline_seed: Light made a flip phone. It’s colorful and it’s cheap.
packet.description_seed: Light co-founder Kaiwei Tang helped create the Motorola Razr, and he's as surprised as anyone that over twenty years later, the flip phone is relevant again.

what: Light made a flip phone. It’s colorful and it’s cheap.

clean_source_blocks.text: Light co-founder Kaiwei Tang helped create the Motorola Razr, and he's as surprised as anyone that over twenty years later, the flip phone is relevant again.

Kaiwei Tang helped create the iconic Motorola Razr over 20 years ago. Now, 10 years into building Light, the startup behind the minimalist smartphone alternative Light Phone, he’s as surprised as anyone that his customers are begging for a flip phone. “We’ve been interviewing young people that use flip phones for a few years,” Tang told TechCrunch, describing a pattern his team kept running into: Gen Z users love their flip phones but say the build quality is bad. “They’re describing the flip phones in negative language, but they stick with it, and they feel proud.” ---

A few years ago, the team at Light shipped the most smartphone-like device they’d ever created. The Light Phone III still kept to its minimalist, no-distractions ethos, but it was a phone-size rectangle with a phone-size touchscreen, a camera, and a number of other features. Some people loved having an almost-smartphone, but Kaiwei Tang, Light’s cofounder, says he started getting feedback he didn’t expect. Lots of users, particularly young ones, didn’t want a smartphone. More than that, actually: They didn’t even want something that looked like a smartphone. “We have users who tell us, ‘Hey, I hate smartphones. I don’t want to be seen using a smartphone,’” Tang says. Then they’d almost always ask for the same thing: a Light Phone, but a flip phone.

Given its form factor, though, the Light Flip does not have a touch screen. Instead, it has a 12-button keypad that'll be familiar to anyone who grew up texting with T9 (or making calls from a landline). There are also three function buttons, the center of which is inside of a four-way directional button to move the phone's cursor around. There's a home button on the side and volume up/down switches surrounding it. Finally, there's a big old speaker at the bottom, a 3.5mm headphone jack and a USB-C port.

It’s not quite a dumbphone, but it’s definitely not a smartphone. And that’s kind of the whole point.

A few years ago, the team at Light shipped the most smartphone-like device they’d ever created. The Light Phone III still kept to its minimalist, no-distractions ethos, but it was a phone-size rectangle with a phone-size touchscreen, a camera, and a number of other features. Some people loved having an almost-smartphone, but Kaiwei Tang, Light’s cofounder, says he started getting feedback he didn’t expect. Lots of users, particularly young ones, didn’t want a smartphone. More than that, actually: They didn’t even want something that looked like a smartphone. “We have users who tell us, ‘Hey, I hate smartphones. I don’t want to be seen using a smartphone,’” Tang says. Then they’d almost always ask for the same thing: a Light Phone, but a flip phone.

So Light made a flip phone, set to ship early next year. “The Light Phone in flip phone form” is even roughly the right way to think about it. This one comes in a bunch of colors – a big departure from the all-black Phone III — but keeps Light’s chunky vibes. There’s a 2.8-inch screen on the top half, but it’s not a touchscreen; all the interaction comes via the bottom half’s standard numberpad, D-pad, and function buttons. The whole thing is powered by a MediaTek MT8873 processor, 128GB of storage, and 6GB of RAM. There’s a USB-C port for charging, a headphone jack for headphones, a single camera on the back, a notification light on the front cover that glows when there’s something for you to see, and not much else.

Early in the process, Tang says, Light decided to really emphasize the flipping of the flip phone. The team opted not to put any kind of screen on the outside of the device, wanting to make sure you had to deliberately open up the device. Tang says he loved “this action of opening up your technology, and then you close it down and it goes away.”

He says the Light Flip is designed mostly as a second phone, not so much to replace your iPhone or Galaxy device entirely but to give you an easy way to leave it at home. That was the idea behind the Light Phone III, too, but that was a hard sell for a $699 device — Tang says most of the negative feedback he’s heard about the Phone III was about its cost. The Light Flip is comparatively priced to move: You can buy it for $299, or you can pay $39 a month

[Lähde: Engadget | URL: https://www.engadget.com/2219683/the-light-flip-is-a-minimalist-flip-phone-that-leaves-out-all-those-distracting-apps/]
It's a mashup of the Light Phone III and an old-school flip phone.

The Brooklyn-based minimalist phone maker Light is working on a new piece of hardware that is decidedly retro. The Light Flip, as the name suggests, is a flip phone that both calls to mind the devices of yesteryear while also combining it with some nods to modernity. A Galaxy Flip-style device this is not, however, In keeping with the company's ethos, the Light Flip is a distraction-free device that has none of the "endless scroll" apps that dominate people's attention.

The Light Flip resembles a mash-up of the Light Phone III (which the company released last year) and an old-school flip phone. In the pictures I've seen so far, the interface closely resembles that of the Light Phone III — it's just a list of tools, white text on a black background. Most of the tools look the same — as I said when I reviewed the Light Phone III last year, this is minimalism taken to the extreme.

Given its form factor, though, the Light Flip does not have a touch screen. Instead, it has a 12-button keypad that'll be familiar to anyone who grew up texting with T9 (or making calls from a landline). There are also three function buttons, the center of which is inside of a four-way directional button to move the phone's cursor around. There's a home button on the side and volume up/down switches surrounding it. Finally, there's a big old speaker at the bottom, a 3.5mm headphone jack and a USB-C port.

Unlike a lot of flip phones both old and new there's no external screen when the Flip is closed. Instead, there's a notification light. On the back, there's a 50-megapixel camera that outputs 12-megapixel images as well as a removeable battery hidden behind a screw-down plate. It's extremely similar to the Light Phone III, though the Flip is made of plastic rather than aluminium. Unlike the Light Phone III, which only comes in black, the Flip will be available in six different shades.

Beyond the new form factor, Light has a few other tricks planned for the Flip. It's the first phone that they'll be selling bundled with a phone plan. $39 a month for two years gets you the Light Flip and the Light service plan with unlimited voice and text plus 1GB of data per month. Given the whole point of the Light Phone is to not use it too much, that data should be good for most buyers. payload.title: Light teki minimalistisen simpukkapuhelimen käyttäjien toiveesta
payload.summary: Light Flip korvaa kosketusnäytön fyysisellä näppäimistöllä. Mallin taustalla on etenkin nuorilta saatu palaute älypuhelinten ulkomuodosta ja nykyisten simpukkapuhelinten rakennuslaadusta.
payload.content:
Minimalistisista Light Phone -laitteistaan tunnettu Light on tehnyt Light Flip -simpukkapuhelimen, jossa kosketusnäyttö on korvattu fyysisillä painikkeilla. Malli syntyi vastauksena etenkin nuorten käyttäjien toiveisiin: osa heistä ei halua älypuhelinta eikä edes älypuhelimelta näyttävää laitetta.

Nuorten käyttäjien palaute muutti suuntaa

Lightin perustajiin kuuluva Kaiwei Tang oli yli 20 vuotta sitten mukana luomassa Motorola Razr -puhelinta. Nyt hän on työskennellyt Lightin parissa kymmenen vuotta ja kertoo yllättyneensä siitä, että asiakkaat pyysivät juuri simpukkapuhelinta. Pyyntö ei koskenut vain puhelimen toimintoja vaan myös sen ulkoista muotoa. Yli kaksi vuosikymmentä myöhemmin sama rakenne on palannut Tangin suunnittelupöydälle asiakaspalautteen vuoksi.

Light on haastatellut simpukkapuhelimia käyttäviä nuoria muutaman vuoden ajan. Tangin kuvaamissa keskusteluissa nuoret ovat pitäneet laitteistaan, vaikka ovat samalla moittineet niiden rakennuslaatua. Kielteisestä palautteesta huolimatta he ovat jatkaneet puhelinten käyttöä ja kokeneet valintansa ylpeydenaiheeksi.

Kosketusnäyttö vaihtui painikkeisiin

Taustalla on Light Phone III, jonka yhtiö teki aiempia laitteitaan enemmän älypuhelimen kaltaiseksi. Siinä on puhelimen kokoinen kosketusnäyttö, kamera ja muita ominaisuuksia, vaikka laite säilytti Lightin minimalistisen ja häiriötekijöitä välttelevän linjan. Osa käyttäjistä piti ratkaisusta, mutta Tangin mukaan moni varsinkin nuori käyttäjä torjui sekä älypuhelimen että sen tutun ulkomuodon.

Palautteen ydin oli Tangin mukaan selvä: käyttäjät eivät halunneet tulla nähdyiksi älypuhelimen kanssa. He pyysivät Light Phonen kaltaista laitetta simpukkapuhelimen muodossa, jotta yhtiön vähäeleinen käyttötapa yhdistyisi selvästi erilaiseen ulkoasuun.

Light Flipissä ei ole kosketusnäyttöä. Sen sijaan laitteessa on 12-painikkeinen näppäimistö, joka muistuttaa T9-tekstiviestien ja lankapuhelinten käyttöä. Lisäksi puhelimessa on kolme toimintopainiketta. Niistä keskimmäinen sijaitsee nelisuuntaisen ohjauspainikkeen sisällä, ja sen avulla näytöllä liikutetaan osoitinta.

Sivulla on kotipainike, jonka ympärille on sijoitettu äänenvoimakkuuden säätimet. Puhelimen alaosassa on suuri kaiutin, ja liitäntöihin kuuluvat 3,5 millimetrin kuulokeliitäntä sekä USB-C-portti. Näin uusi malli toteuttaa käyttäjien pyytämän Light Phonen simpukkapuhelimen muodossa.

Light Flipissä ei ole kosketusnäyttöä. Sen sijaan laitteessa on 12-painikkeinen näppäimistö, joka muistuttaa T9-tekstiviestien ja lankapuhelinten käyttöä. Lisäksi puhelimessa on kolme toimintopainiketta. Niistä keskimmäinen sijaitsee nelisuuntaisen ohjauspainikkeen sisällä, ja sen avulla näytöllä liikutetaan osoitinta.

Sivulla on kotipainike, jonka ympärille on sijoitettu äänenvoimakkuuden säätimet. Puhelimen alaosassa on suuri kaiutin, ja liitäntöihin kuuluvat 3,5 millimetrin kuulokeliitäntä sekä USB-C-portti. Näin uusi malli toteuttaa käyttäjien pyytämän Light Phonen simpukkapuhelimen muodossa.

article.source_text:
Light co-founder Kaiwei Tang helped create the Motorola Razr, and he's as surprised as anyone that over twenty years later, the flip phone is relevant again.

Kaiwei Tang helped create the iconic Motorola Razr over 20 years ago. Now, 10 years into building Light, the startup behind the minimalist smartphone alternative Light Phone, he’s as surprised as anyone that his customers are begging for a flip phone. “We’ve been interviewing young people that use flip phones for a few years,” Tang told TechCrunch, describing a pattern his team kept running into: Gen Z users love their flip phones but say the build quality is bad. “They’re describing the flip phones in negative language, but they stick with it, and they feel proud.” ---

A few years ago, the team at Light shipped the most smartphone-like device they’d ever created. The Light Phone III still kept to its minimalist, no-distractions ethos, but it was a phone-size rectangle with a phone-size touchscreen, a camera, and a number of other features. Some people loved having an almost-smartphone, but Kaiwei Tang, Light’s cofounder, says he started getting feedback he didn’t expect. Lots of users, particularly young ones, didn’t want a smartphone. More than that, actually: They didn’t even want something that looked like a smartphone. “We have users who tell us, ‘Hey, I hate smartphones. I don’t want to be seen using a smartphone,’” Tang says. Then they’d almost always ask for the same thing: a Light Phone, but a flip phone.

Given its form factor, though, the Light Flip does not have a touch screen. Instead, it has a 12-button keypad that'll be familiar to anyone who grew up texting with T9 (or making calls from a landline). There are also three function buttons, the center of which is inside of a four-way directional button to move the phone's cursor around. There's a home button on the side and volume up/down switches surrounding it. Finally, there's a big old speaker at the bottom, a 3.5mm headphone jack and a USB-C port.
